title: Habakkuk 1:1–4
context: The book opens with a heading that presents what follows as “The revelation which Habakkuk the prophet saw” (1:1). Unlike most prophetic books, Habakkuk begins with the prophet speaking to God about the people rather than to the people for God. In this first complaint Habakkuk asks how long he must cry out about violence, strife, and perverted justice before the LORD acts (1:2–4). Most readers take the violence as injustice within Judah, though some see foreign oppression here. The book names the Chaldeans, that is, the Babylonians, as a rising power (1:6), and many date it to the late seventh century BC, perhaps in the reign of Jehoiakim, but no king is named and the precise date is uncertain. Little is known of Habakkuk beyond this book. Shared ground: both traditions read the complaint as faithful lament rather than unbelief, and both value the book’s movement from honest questions, through the LORD’s answers, to trust and joy in chapter 3.

verses.text: The revelation which Habakkuk the prophet saw.
verses.arminianNotes: “The revelation which Habakkuk the prophet saw.” The heading presents what follows as something Habakkuk received, not invented. Arminian readers note that the revelation unfolds through a real dialogue in which the prophet’s questions are welcomed and answered, a sign of the relational way God deals with his servants.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that the message is a “revelation” that Habakkuk “saw”: its source is God, and the prophet’s honest questions are themselves part of the inspired word. Shared ground: both traditions read the heading as claiming divine origin, note that little is known of Habakkuk beyond this book, and value its pattern of lament, answer, and trust.

verses.text: LORD, how long will I cry, and you will not hear? I cry out to you “Violence!” and will you not save?
verses.arminianNotes: “LORD, how long will I cry, and you will not hear?” Habakkuk prays with startling honesty. Arminian readers value the freedom this models: believers may bring raw complaint to God, and the delay of an answer is a real trial within a genuine relationship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same honesty as faith wrestling within God’s sovereign purposes; the apparent silence is not absence, as the LORD’s answer in verse 5 will show. Shared ground: both traditions treat the lament as faithful prayer rather than unbelief (compare Psalm 13:1–2), and both read “how long” as a cry for justice rooted in trust that the LORD can act.

verses.text: Why do you show me iniquity, and look at perversity? For destruction and violence are before me. There is strife, and contention rises up.
verses.arminianNotes: “Why do you show me iniquity, and look at perversity?” Arminian readers hear a prophet troubled that God seems to tolerate wrong, and they see the question as legitimate: the problem of evil is felt most keenly by those who believe that God is good.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Habakkuk does not doubt God’s control; rather, because God governs all things, the prophet asks why he lets destruction and strife stand before his eyes. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the cry of faith confronting evil, and both affirm that God’s goodness, not his indifference, is what makes the question so painful.

verses.text: Therefore the law is paralyzed, and justice never prevails; for the wicked surround the righteous; therefore justice comes out perverted.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore the law is paralyzed, and justice never prevails.” Arminian readers see a society in which the wicked have chosen to surround the righteous, so that justice is perverted through human corruption, and they hear the prophet appealing to God to set it right.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize the collapse of God’s law, his covenant instruction, as the root of the disorder, and see perverted justice as the fruit of hearts that do not fear the LORD. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse most naturally as injustice within Judah, note that some readers see foreign oppression here instead, and agree that God cares when justice fails.
